what: Granite Construction builds and maintains infrastructure. It constructs and resurfaces highways, builds bridges, tunnels and water systems, and it also quarries and sells the aggregates and asphalt that go into those projects.
customers: State transportation departments, federal agencies, municipalities and water authorities, plus private customers buying aggregates and asphalt from its quarries.
money: Highway, bridge, tunnel and water infrastructure projects, mostly for public clients.
Aggregates, asphalt and ready-mix concrete, the higher-margin segment.
moat: The materials business is the quality asset: a quarry is a permitted, fixed-location resource, aggregates are too heavy to ship far, and new quarry permits are extremely difficult to obtain — so each one is a local monopoly. Construction itself is competitive bidding, where the advantage is local presence, bonding capacity and owning the materials your own projects need.
risks: A trailing net loss of $264.6M, which in construction usually means a project or legacy claim has gone badly wrong.
Fixed-price construction contracting is the industry’s historical destroyer of capital: one badly estimated project can consume years of profit.
Debt of $1.5B against $600.2M of cash is meaningful for a business with project risk of this kind.
Public infrastructure spending depends on government budgets and funding bills, which are political.
Only six analysts cover the stock, and their $173.33 average against a $116.17 price is a 49% gap.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $443.2M against a $5.1B market value is an 8.7% yield, and the shares trade at about 11.6 times free cash flow.
Revenue has grown every year, from $3.3B in 2022 to $4.4B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $5.3B.
Quarries are permitted local monopolies: aggregates cannot be shipped far and new permits are nearly impossible to obtain.
Owning the materials its own projects consume captures margin that a pure contractor pays away.
Federal infrastructure funding supports multi-year highway and water programmes.
watch: The materials segment’s revenue and margin, and the mix of fixed-price work in the backlog. Materials is the durable value; contract type is what determines whether construction destroys it.
view: Granite is two businesses with opposite risk profiles, and the market tends to value it as the worse one. Construction is competitive bidding on highway, bridge and tunnel projects, where a single mis-estimated fixed-price job can consume several years of profit — and the trailing net loss of $265 million suggests exactly that has happened. This is not unusual; it is the characteristic failure mode of the entire industry.

The materials business is genuinely excellent and gets far less attention than it deserves. A quarry is a permitted, fixed-location deposit, aggregates are too heavy to ship economically beyond a short radius, and obtaining a permit for a new quarry in the United States is close to impossible. That makes every existing quarry a local monopoly with pricing power. Vulcan and Martin Marietta are valued at premium multiples precisely because this is what they are, and Granite owns a slice of the same thing.

There is also a structural advantage in owning both: Granite’s construction projects consume aggregates and asphalt, and buying them from itself captures margin that a pure contractor pays away to a supplier. That vertical integration is a real edge in bidding, because it lowers the true cost of a project relative to competitors who must buy materials at market.

At 11.6 times free cash flow with an 8.7% yield, the price reflects the construction loss rather than the materials franchise. What would change my view in either direction is the mix of fixed-price work in the backlog — Granite’s history, like the industry’s, says contract type matters more than backlog size. If management is shifting toward reimbursable and best-value work while growing the materials segment, this is a considerably better business than the trailing loss suggests. Six analysts covering a $5.1 billion company means few people are checking.
bull: Federal infrastructure funding fills the backlog while permitted quarries earn local-monopoly margins, and a shift away from fixed-price work ends the project losses.
bear: Another fixed-price project goes wrong, legacy claims keep consuming cash, and $1.5 billion of debt meets a construction business that cannot price risk.
